claim: Macromolecular X-ray diffraction can provide information on both anharmonic and harmonic contributions to conformational heterogeneity.
source: Macromolecular X-ray diffraction is commonly interpreted with a static structure, but it can provide information on both the anharmonic and harmonic contributions to conformational heterogeneity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a property of X-ray diffraction data.

claim: The study analyzed 743 stringently matched pairs of crystallographic datasets reflecting unbound/apo and ligand-bound/holo states.
source: Here, through multiconformer modeling of time- and space-averaged electron density, we measure conformational heterogeneity of 743 stringently matched pairs of crystallographic datasets that reflect unbound/apo and ligand-bound/holo states.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of matched pairs analyzed in the study.

claim: When binding site residues become more rigid upon ligand binding, distant residues tend to become more flexible, especially in non-solvent-exposed regions.
source: When comparing the conformational heterogeneity of side chains, we observe that when binding site residues become more rigid upon ligand binding, distant residues tend to become more flexible, especially in non-solvent-exposed regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data analysis in the results section.

claim: Increased protein flexibility is observed as the number of hydrogen bonds decreases and relative hydrophobicity increases.
source: Among ligand properties, we observe increased protein flexibility as the number of hydrogen bonds decreases and relative hydrophobicity increases.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by ligand property analysis in the results.

claim: Conformational heterogeneity is correlated with inhibitor features in CDK2 structures.
source: Across a series of 13 inhibitor-bound structures of CDK2, we find that conformational heterogeneity is correlated with inhibitor features and identify how conformational changes propagate differences in conformational heterogeneity away from the binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through analysis of 13 CDK2 structures in the results.

claim: Ligand binding reshapes the protein conformational ensemble between the ligand-bound (holo) and unbound (apo) states.
source: Ligand binding reshapes the protein conformational ensemble between the ligand-bound (holo) and unbound (apo) states, stabilizing some conformations and destabilizing others (Boehr et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Protein conformational entropy can contribute between –2 (favoring) and 4 (disfavoring) kcal/mol to binding free energy.
source: Previous work examining a diverse set of protein complexes calculated that protein conformational entropy can contribute between –2 (favoring) and 4 (disfavoring) kcal/mol to binding free energy (Caro et al., 2021; Caro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Side-chain conformational heterogeneity measured by NMR relaxation studies has been linked to entropy.
source: Side-chain conformational heterogeneity, including jumps between and variation within rotameric conformations, measured by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) relaxation studies has been linked to entropy (Caro et al., 2021; Frederick et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to NMR studies.

claim: When averaged in a single-density map, conformational heterogeneity can manifest as 'anharmonic disorder' modeled using multiple alternative conformations, or 'harmonic disorder' modeled by B-factors.
source: When averaged in a single-density map, conformational heterogeneity across these copies can manifest as 'anharmonic disorder,' which can be modeled using multiple alternative conformations, or 'harmonic disorder,' which can be modeled by B-factors/atomic displacement parameters (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explained in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: If alternative conformations are not modeled correctly and consistently, B-factors take on values that are not representative of the underlying conformational heterogeneity.
source: Molecular dynamics experiments have demonstrated that if alternative conformations are not modeled correctly and consistently, then B-factors take on values that are not representative of the underlying conformational heterogeneity (Kuzmanic et al., 2014; Kuriyan et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to molecular dynamics studies.

claim: The dataset contained 1205 pairs after initial selection criteria were applied.
source: This stringently matched ligand holo-apo dataset contained 1205 pairs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing dataset assembly.

claim: A control dataset of 293 apo-apo pairs was created using identical selection criteria.
source: We also used identical selection criteria to create a control dataset of 293 apo-apo pairs, taken from the set of apo/holo pairs (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing dataset assembly.

claim: The majority of structures in the re-refined dataset had less than 2% of residues modeled with alternative conformations.
source: The majority of structures in our re-refined dataset had less than 2% of residues modeled with alternative conformations, likely reflecting undermodeling of conformational heterogeneity represented in the PDB, based on prior literature (Lang et al., 2010).
evidence: This observation is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: After quality control, the final dataset contained 743 pairs.
source: This procedure resulted in 743 pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section after describing the quality control process.

claim: The dataset consists of 743 unique holo structures and 432 unique apo structures.
source: Due to apo datasets serving as the reference state for multiple ligand-bound structures, our dataset consists of 743 unique holo structures and 432 unique apo structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the dataset properties.

claim: The median resolution across the dataset was 1.6 Å.
source: The median resolution across our dataset was 1.6 Å with a small trend towards improved (higher) resolution in the apo structure (0.01 Å, median improvement [holo-apo]; p=3.8 × 10–20, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: 546 unique ligands were present in the structures.
source: Across the dataset, 546 unique ligands were present in the structures, with 134 of these (e.g., NAG, AMP) appearing in multiple structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The median number of ligand heavy atoms was 19.
source: The median number of ligand heavy atoms was 19, with only 10 very large ligands (>50 heavy atoms, e.g., atazanavir; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The proteins in the dataset represent 315 unique UniProt IDs.
source: The proteins in the dataset represent 315 unique UniProt IDs, with a bias towards enzymes that have been used for model systems for structural biology, including endothiopepsin (n = 73 pairs), lysozyme (n = 62 pairs), trypsin (n = 48 pairs), and carbonic anhydrase 2 (n = 46 pairs; Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and D.

claim: Alternative conformations were modeled at low frequency in the re-refined dataset compared to the qFit modeled structures (1.7% vs. 47.8% of residues).
source: Alternative conformations were modeled at low frequency in the re-refined dataset compared to the qFit modeled structures (1.7% vs. 47.8% of residues).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the re-refined dataset, there is a bias to increased modeling of alternative conformations in the holo dataset (50.5% gain vs. 29.8% loss).
source: In the re-refined dataset, there is a bias to increased modeling of alternative conformations in the holo dataset (50.5% gain vs. 29.8% loss), whereas more even representation was observed in the qFit dataset (44.3% gain vs. 54.8% loss; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: In the qFit dataset, holo models tend to lose alternative conformations in the binding site residues (39.7% gain vs. 51.5% loss).
source: However, in the qFit dataset, holo models tend to lose alternative conformations in the binding site residues (39.7% gain vs. 51.5% loss; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Across all residues in the re-refined dataset, B-factors were slightly higher in holo models (0.31 Å2, median difference [holo-apo]; p=4.4 × 10–208, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: Across all residues in the re-refined dataset, B-factors were slightly higher in holo models (0.31 Å2, median difference [holo-apo]; p=4.4 × 10–208, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: In the qFit dataset, holo residues had slightly higher B-factors (0.34 Å2, median difference [holo-apo]; p=5.6 × 10–264, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: In the qFit dataset, similar to the re-refined structures, holo residues had slightly higher B-factors (0.34 Å2, median difference [holo-apo]; p=5.6 × 10–264, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A.

claim: There was no significant difference in B-factors between the holo and apo models in binding site residues in both the re-refined and qFit datasets.
source: When examining the binding site residues, there was no significant difference in B-factors between the holo and apo models in both the re-refined (0.01 Å2, median difference in B-factors; p=0.34, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1D) and qFit datasets (0.06 Å2, median difference in B-factors; p=0.7, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 6B.

claim: 90% of binding sites have at least one residue changing rotamers upon ligand binding in single-conformer models.
source: Side-chain rotamer changes between apo and holo structures have been reported to be very prevalent in single-conformer models, with 90% of binding sites having at least one residue changing rotamers upon ligand binding (Gaudreault et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 'No change' in rotamers was the most common outcome for binding site residues (78.6%).
source: In binding sites, we also observed that 'no change' was the most common outcome for residues (78.6%; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the second largest category, 'distinct,' the holo and apo residues shared no rotamer assignments (15.5% of residues).
source: In the second largest category, 'distinct,' the holo and apo residues shared no rotamer assignments (15.5% of residues; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 2.6% of residues were classified as 'remodeled-holo loss'.
source: We classified 2.6% of residues as 'remodeled-holo loss' (Figure 2C) if distinct, additional rotameric conformations were populated in the apo residue only and 3.8% of residues as 'remodeled-holo gain' (Figure 2D) if distinct, additional rotameric conformations were populated in the holo residue only.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 3.8% of residues were classified as 'remodeled-holo gain'.
source: We classified 2.6% of residues as 'remodeled-holo loss' (Figure 2C) if distinct, additional rotameric conformations were populated in the apo residue only and 3.8% of residues as 'remodeled-holo gain' (Figure 2D) if distinct, additional rotameric conformations were populated in the holo residue only.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 11% of binding sites had all residues classified as 'same' between pairs.
source: We found that 11% of binding sites had all residues classified as 'same' between pairs, consistent with a previous study that used single-conformer models (Gaudreault et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: On average, apo residues have slightly greater conformational heterogeneity than holo residues (–0.006 Å, mean difference of RMSF(holo-apo); p=3.7 × 10–8, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: This analysis suggested that, on average, apo residues have slightly greater conformational heterogeneity than holo residues (–0.006 Å, mean difference of RMSF(holo-apo); p=3.7 × 10–8, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The RMSF trend was somewhat stronger in binding site residues (–0.02 Å, mean difference of RMSF(holo-apo); p=4.5 × 10–29, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: This trend was somewhat stronger in binding site residues (–0.02 Å, mean difference of RMSF(holo-apo); p=4.5 × 10–29, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the apo/holo pairs there is a much wider range of order parameter differences compared to apo/apo pairs (p=3.4 × 10–17, individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: However, in the apo/holo pairs there is a much wider range of order parameter differences, indicating that ligand binding impacts conformational heterogeneity beyond experimental variability (p=3.4 × 10–17, individual Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 3A).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In binding site residues, the holo structures had a slightly, but significantly, increased order parameters compared to the control dataset (0.034 vs. 0, median difference [holo-apo] order parameter; p=3.4 × 10–7, individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: In binding site residues, the holo structures had a slightly, but significantly, increased order parameters, suggesting reduced conformational heterogeneity compared to the control dataset (0.034 vs. 0, median difference [holo-apo] order parameter; p=3.4 × 10–7, individual Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 3B).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relationship between binding site residues and residual changes at distant sites shows an inverse trend (slope = −0.44, r2 = 0.46; p=5.1 × 10–50, two-sided t-test).
source: Consistent with studies suggesting significant residual conformational heterogeneity in folded buried residues (Wong and Daggett, 1998) and the potential for those buried residues to change heterogeneity upon ligand binding (Moorman et al., 2012), this trend is even stronger in residues that were more than 10 Å away from any heavy atom in the ligand and less than 20% solvent exposed (slope = −0.44, r2 = 0.46; p=5.1 × 10–50, two-sided t-test; Figure 3C).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C, with supporting citations.

claim: In apo-apo pairs, the trends were similar but weaker in both correlation and magnitude (slope = −0.28, r2 = 0.20; p=1.8 × 10–34, two-sided t-test).
source: As a control for these effects, we compared the residual order parameter differences between the buried, non-solvent-exposed residues and the binding site residues in apo-apo pairs. Globally the trends were similar, but weaker in both correlation and magnitude (slope = −0.28, r2 = 0.20; p=1.8 × 10–34, two-sided t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The mean slope of the holo-apo is more than 2 standard deviations away from the apo-apo slope (p=0.0, z-test).
source: The difference in the slope between the holo-apo and apo-apo dataset was further compared using a bootstrap analysis, demonstrating that the mean slope of the holo-apo is more than 2 standard deviations away from the apo-apo slope, representing the robustness in differences between the two slopes (p=0.0, z-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The creation of 0.06 hydrogen bonds per residue in holo binding sites was observed, which translates to 10% of structures gaining one full hydrogen bond in the holo structure.
source: Overall, we observed the creation of 0.06 hydrogen bonds per residue in holo binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which translates to 10% of structures gaining one full hydrogen bond in the holo structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Higher lipophilicity (logP) was significantly associated with a more flexible binding site (0.79 vs. 0.84, median order parameters; p=7.5 × 10–6, individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: Increased lipophilicity (logP, upper quartile: <0.04 [n = 134] vs. lower quartile: >2.69 [n = 134]) was significantly associated with a more flexible binding site (0.79 vs. 0.84, median order parameters; p=7.5 × 10–6, individual Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 4A).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Larger compounds are associated with more flexible binding sites (0.83 vs. 0.79, median order parameter; p=0.0001, individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: Larger compounds (upper quartile: >26 heavy atoms [n = 134] vs. lower quartile: <13 heavy atoms [n = 134]) are also associated with more flexible binding sites (0.83 vs. 0.79, median order parameter; p=0.0001, individual Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 4B).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: More total hydrogen bonds per heavy atom are associated with more rigid binding sites (0.84 vs. 0.79, median order parameter; p=5.9 × 10–5, individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: Finally, more total hydrogen bonds per heavy atom (upper quartile: >0.47 [n = 134] vs. lower quartile: <0.25 [n = 134]) are associated with more rigid binding sites (0.84 vs. 0.79, median order parameter; p=5.9 × 10–5, individual Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 4C).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were 193 structures with ligands with alternative conformations or partially occupied ligands in the datasets.
source: There were 193 structures with ligands with alternative conformations or partially occupied ligands in our datasets (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fully occupied ligands were associated with more rigid binding sites than partially occupied ligands or ligands with alternative conformers (0.84 vs. 0.79, mean order parameters of binding site residues; p=2.9 × 10–7, individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: Fully occupied ligands were associated with more rigid binding sites than partially occupied ligands or ligands with alternative conformers (0.84 vs. 0.79, mean order parameters of binding site residues; p=2.9 × 10–7, individual Mann–Whitney U test; Figure 4D).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In 'likely partially occupied' ligands, greater conformational heterogeneity was observed (0.86 vs. 0.80, mean order parameter; p=1.6 × 10–11; individual Mann–Whitney U test).
source: In these 'likely partially occupied' ligands, we observed greater conformational heterogeneity (0.86 vs. 0.80, mean order parameter; p=1.6 × 10–11; individual Mann–Whitney U test, Figure 4E).
evidence: This statistical result is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The CDK2 dataset contains 13 protein inhibitor complexes, including both type I and type II inhibitors, all sharing the same apo model (PDB ID: 1PW2).
source: Our dataset contains 13 protein inhibitor complexes, including both type I and type II inhibitors, all of which share the same apo model (PDB ID: 1PW2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the CDK2 analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of CDK2 residues and ligands by difference in order parameters identified three distinct clusters of residues.
source: We hierarchically clustered the residues and ligands by difference in order parameters between the holo and apo models, identifying three distinct clusters of residues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the CDK2 analysis.

claim: The first cluster (blue) consisting of 13 residues is rigidified upon ligand binding.
source: The first cluster (blue, Figure 5A and B), consisting of 13 residues, is rigidified upon ligand binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The second cluster (salmon) consists of 14 residues that increase flexibility upon ligand binding.
source: The second cluster (salmon, Figure 5A and B) consists of 14 residues that increase flexibility upon ligand binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The third cluster (dark red) comprises five residues that became more flexible in all but two holo datasets, which are the only type II inhibitors in the dataset.
source: The third cluster (dark red, Figure 5A and B) comprises five residues that became more flexible in all, but two holo datasets, which are the only type II inhibitors in the dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The median increase in rigidity observed in binding site residues (0.03 order parameter increase) would create an energetic penalty of approximately ~0.1–0.5 kcal/mol.
source: Overall, the median increase in rigidity we observe in binding site residues (0.03 order parameter increase) would create an energetic penalty of approximately ~0.1–0.5 kcal/mol, based off of the entropy meter calculated in Caro et al., 2017 and Caro et al., 2021, with outliers having even larger thermodynamic consequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and based on calculations from cited studies.

claim: Restricting the rotamer of even a single side chain can incur an entropic penalty of binding of ~0.5 kcal/mol.
source: Protein folding studies and theory indicate that restricting the rotamer of even a single side chain can incur an entropic penalty of binding of ~0.5 kcal/mol (Doig and Sternberg, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to protein folding studies.

claim: The use of cryo-cooled structures likely causes an underestimate of the heterogeneity occurring in these datasets.
source: In addition, it is quite likely that our use of cryo-cooled structures causes an underestimate of the heterogeneity occurring in these datasets (Fraser et al., 2011), and may potentially bias our results by locking in certain populations of the protein ensemble.
evidence: This limitation is discussed in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Holo structures were required to have a ligand with 10 or more heavy atoms.
source: Holo structures (n = 30,530) were required to have a ligand, not including common crystallographic additives, with 10 or more heavy atoms.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing dataset assembly.

claim: All structures went through re-refinement using phenix.refine.
source: To minimize biases resulting from different model refinement protocols, we re-refined all structures using the deposited structure factors and phenix.refine (Liebschner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the refinement procedure.

claim: qFit-3.0 was run using a composite omit map and the re-refined structure on the default parameters.
source: qFit-3.0 (Riley et al., 2021a; version 3.2.0) was run using a composite omit map and the re-refined structure on the default parameters (https://github.com/ExcitedStates/qfit-3.0/).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the qFit procedure.

claim: Order parameters were measured for each residue (except proline and glycine) by taking into account both the angle of alternative conformers and the B-factors.
source: Order parameters were measured for each residue (except proline and glycine) by taking into account both the angle of alternative conformers (s2angle), by measuring the chi1 angle, and the B-factors of alpha or beta carbons along with an attached hydrogen(s2ortho) (Fenwick et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing order parameter calculation.

claim: Binding site residues were defined as any residue with a heavy atom within 5 Å of any ligand heavy atom.
source: We next focused our analysis on binding site residues, defined as any residue with a heavy atom within 5 Å of any ligand heavy atom.
evidence: This definition is stated in the Results section.

claim: Residues with a RASA of ≥20% were considered solvent exposed.
source: Residues with a RASA of ≥20% were considered solvent exposed (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This definition is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation.

claim: Increased lipophilicity generates more nonspecific binding interactions.
source: Previous studies have indicated that increased lipophilicity generates more nonspecific binding interactions (Olsson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous studies.

claim: More specific, directional interactions, such as hydrogen bonds, are more likely to lock the corresponding protein residue in place, thus creating more rigid binding site residues.
source: From these results, an intuitive general picture emerges where more specific, directional interactions, such as hydrogen bonds (Bissantz et al., 2010), are more likely to lock the corresponding protein residue in place, thus creating more rigid binding site residues (Majewski et al., 2019).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Upon ligand binding, hydrogen bonds to water molecules decrease, but hydrogen bonds to other protein atoms increase.
source: This follows a trend observed previously where upon ligand binding, hydrogen bonds to water molecules decrease, but hydrogen bonds to other protein atoms increase (Gaudreault et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ligand binding generally acts to restrict degrees of freedom locally and protein topological constraints favor increased motion in distal regions.
source: Given the constraints of maintaining a folded conformational ensemble upon ligand binding, it is likely that ligand binding generally acts to restrict degrees of freedom locally and that protein topological constraints favor increased motion in distal regions (Bromberg and Dill, 1994).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.
